sections.h2: What should I know about property tax in Randolph County, Missouri?
sections.html:
Randolph County property tax is billed by the county Collector and valued by the county Assessor, both in the courthouse at Huntsville. Real estate is valued as of January 1, bills go out in the fall, and the whole amount is due by December 31.

The county sits in north-central Missouri, covers 488 square miles and was organized on January 22, 1829. Moberly is the largest city. Huntsville is the seat, and the other incorporated places are Clark, Clifton Hill and Higbee, plus the villages of Cairo, Jacksonville and Renick. The county borders Macon, Monroe, Shelby, Audrain, Boone, Howard and Chariton counties, and U.S. 24, U.S. 63 and Route 3 cross it. The Census Bureau counted 24,716 people in 2020 and estimates 24,513 for July 1, 2025.

School district matters on a tax bill. Houses here fall in the Moberly School District, Westran R-I at Huntsville, Higbee R-VIII, Northeast Randolph County R-IV at Cairo or Renick R-V, and each district sets its own levy. Look at the district line on your own statement before comparing one Randolph County address with another.

sections.h2: Which Randolph County offices handle my tax questions?
sections.html:
Every county office is at 372 Hwy. JJ in Huntsville, MO 65259. Most are open weekdays from 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m., and the main number is 844-277-6555 with an extension for each office. The county site links to the Collector's and Assessor's own web pages.

  • Collector: Michelle Lee, courthouse Suite 1G, extension 310. Collects current and delinquent real estate and personal property tax and distributes it to schools, cities, the library, ambulance and fire districts.
  • Assessor: sets values and handles address changes. Property records are searchable through the link on the county home page.
  • County Clerk: the office to ask for board of equalization forms and deadlines.
  • County Commission: meets on Tuesdays and Wednesdays at 9 a.m., with agendas posted on the county site.

The Collector's office also answers mortgage companies that need tax figures or pay from escrow. If you do not find your statement online, the Collector's page tells you to call the Assessor, because statements are now posted online.

sections.h2: How does Randolph County assess a house?
sections.html:
The Assessor values a house at its market price and then taxes only a share of that value. Under RSMo 137.115, a residential parcel is assessed at 19 percent of true value, farm ground at 12 percent and commercial property at 32 percent.

New values are set as of January 1 of every odd-numbered year and carry into the even year after, except for new construction and improvements. Because 2027 is an odd year, a fresh valuation for Randolph County homes will be set as of January 1, 2027. If the Assessor raises a residential parcel by more than 15 percent, other than for new building, the statute requires a physical inspection, and the owner may ask for the inside of the house to be viewed too.

sections.h2: When is Randolph County property tax due, and how do I pay?
sections.html:
Pay by December 31. The Collector accepts payment at the courthouse, by mail, in the drop box at the front of the building, at the drive-up window or online with Discover, MasterCard or Visa. Online payments carry a convenience fee that the county does not keep, and the page shows the amount before you confirm.

Mailed payments count on their postmark date. RSMo 139.100 treats a payment delivered by U.S. mail as paid on the postmark, and a postal error does not cost you a penalty if the postmaster verifies it in writing. An unpaid bill after January 1 picks up the penalty set in RSMo 140.100. That section charges eighteen percent of each year's delinquency on land in the back tax book, and no more than two percent per month on land redeemed before a sale.

  • The online system makes you pay the oldest delinquent year before the current one.
  • Missing a statement does not remove the duty to pay on time.
  • Receipts can be downloaded after a search by name, account number or parcel number.

sections.h2: How do I appeal a Randolph County assessment?
sections.html:
Start with the Assessor, then go to the board of equalization, then to the State Tax Commission. The commission's own guide says to contact the county Assessor's office as soon as you get notice, ask how the value was reached and bring evidence of market value.

If that does not settle it, ask the County Clerk for the board of equalization forms and filing dates. The board decides appeals in a summary way, and RSMo 138.060 says nothing presumes the Assessor's value is correct. A further appeal goes to the State Tax Commission by September 30 or within 30 days after the board's final action, whichever is later, under RSMo 138.430.

Evidence matters more than complaints about the bill. The commission says that saying taxes are too high is not relevant testimony, while a recent sale, photographs or an appraisal are. A taxpayer who wants to protest the tax itself pays the full bill before the delinquency date and files a written statement with the Collector, then has ninety days to sue under RSMo 139.031.

sections.h2: What happens to the tax bill when I sell a Randolph County house?
sections.html:
Ask the Collector for the current balance before you sign a contract, and expect the closing agent to split the year's tax between you and the buyer. The state sets the January 1 assessment date, so the bill follows the parcel through the year even when the house changes hands.

A few steps keep a sale from stalling over tax:

  • Request a written statement of current and any delinquent amounts from the Collector at Suite 1G.
  • Give the title company the parcel number from the Assessor's record.
  • Tell the Collector and Assessor the buyer's mailing address after closing, so the next bill goes to the right person.
  • If a mortgage company pays from escrow, confirm the payment posted before you list.

Owners with back taxes, an inherited house or a vacant property in Moberly, Huntsville or one of the villages sometimes choose a cash sale to close in a few weeks. A cash buyer still needs the same payoff figures, so the Collector's statement is the first document to request in every case.

faqs.q: Where do I pay Randolph County property tax?
faqs.a: At the Collector's office in courthouse Suite 1G, 372 Hwy. JJ, Huntsville, by mail, in the drop box, at the drive-up window or online. Office hours are 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. on weekdays, and the phone is 844-277-6555 extension 310.

faqs.q: What is the deadline for Randolph County property tax?
faqs.a: December 31. A mailed payment is on time if the U.S. postmark is dated on or before that day. After January 1 the penalty under RSMo 140.100 applies.

faqs.q: What percent of my home's value is taxed in Randolph County?
faqs.a: Nineteen percent for residential property under RSMo 137.115. Farm land is assessed at 12 percent and commercial property at 32 percent, and the tax rate for your school and levy district is applied to that assessed value.

faqs.q: How often does Randolph County reassess homes?
faqs.a: Every two years. New values are set as of January 1 of each odd-numbered year, so the next general valuation is as of January 1, 2027, and the same values generally carry into 2028 unless the property is improved.

faqs.q: Can I appeal if I miss the county board of equalization date?
faqs.a: Possibly. A complaint to the State Tax Commission is due by September 30 or within 30 days of the board's final action, whichever is later, so a late board date can still leave time. Call the County Clerk right away for the board's dates.
